item.content:encoded:
Justin Verlander, David Ortiz Put Their MLB Memories To The Test In 'Fact Or Splat'
Between the two of them, David Ortiz and Justin Verlander have a combined five World Series rings, 20 All-Star appearances and 3,088 games played in MLB. So, recalling facts about their own illustrious careers shouldn't be too hard for them, right?
Their memories were put to the test in a new game called "Fact Or Splat," with some help from Derek Jeter and Alex Rodriguez. The rules are simple: If you get the answer right, you get to drop a fruit on a giant cutout of your opponent's face; if you get it wrong, your opponent gets to drop the fruit.
How did Verlander and Big Papi do? Let's see the results:
Big Papi & Justin Verlander Take on MESSIEST MLB Trivia Challenge FACT or SPLAT
Jeter gave the hint, "It’s someone that’s in the family." Ortiz immediately knew the answer: former Dominican right-hander Ramon Martinez.
The cake was a direct hit.
Next, it was Verlander’s turn to answer his first question.
Jeter asked, "Who was your first strikeout victim ever in your career?"
The recently retired right-hander did not hesitate: "Travis Hafner."
It was a fast answer, but Verlander’s toss did not make nearly as impressive contact with Ortiz’s face.
Next up: "Papi, this one’s for you. Who was your longest-tenured teammate?"
Ortiz played 20 years in the majors, 14 of which came in Boston. It could have been any number of players.
The answer? Dustin Pedroia. Ortiz’s guess was knuckleballer Tim Wakefield.
Verlander got better on his second toss and made a direct hit on Ortiz’s face.
Verlander looked around and said, "I’m going to go with Derek."
The ace nailed it, and down went a pumpkin onto Big Papi’s face.
Papi didn’t need much time to answer this one.
"Manny Ramirez, Mikey Lowell and myself," he answered before cake went falling on Verlander’s face.
Verlander got Max Scherzer, Rick Porcello, Tarik Skubal (he got a generous hint from A-Rod to get him) and Gerrit Cole.
The four players who Verlander missed: Dallas Keuchel, Zack Greinke, David Price and Robbie Ray.

Manny Ramirez Eyes MLB Coaching Role, Red Sox Legend Hit 555 Career HR
Manny Ramírez was one of MLB's best hitters during his playing career. Now, he's hoping to parlay that accumulated knowledge into a coaching role.
According to Jon Heyman of the New York Post, Ramírez is seeking a job as a hitting coach, either at the MLB or minor league level:
TOP NEWS
Players Who Were Worse Than You Think in 2026 ⚾
Sox Brass Met With Contreras
Latest Free Agent Rumors 👂
It is not the first time Ramírez's agent has let this be publicly known. In fact, it was almost exactly one year ago that Heyman posted the following:
"I'm available to work as a hitting coach for any of the 30 MLB teams," Ramírez said back in May 2025. "I'm confident I can help any team significantly improve their offense."
Ramírez, 54, hit .312 with 2,574 hits, 555 home runs, 1,831 RBI and a .996 OPS during his 19-year MLB career. The two-time World Series champion, 12-time All-Star and nine-time Silver Slugger would assuredly be a Hall of Famer were it not for the three separate positive tests for performance-enhancing drugs during his career.
But there's little doubt the man knew how to swing a bat at the highest level. Whether that would translate to teaching others and helping big leaguers make the necessary adjustments throughout a season is another question entirely.

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the Red Sox bringing in franchise legend Manny Ramirez as a hitting instructor. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
For 19 years, Manny Ramirez terrorized pitchers as one of the greatest right-handed hitters of all-time. Now, he's reportedly looking for a job as a hitting coach in Major League Baseball.
"Manny Ramirez is seeking a hitting coach job in MLB, agent Hector Zepeda said," tweeted Jon Heyman of the New York Post on Monday afternoon. "He's so determined to get back in the game he's willing to go to the minors," he continued.
Ramirez spent 19 seasons in the big leagues, hitting .312/.411/.585/.996 with 555 career home runs. He spent eight years with the Boston Red Sox, where he hit .312/.411/.588/.999 with 274 home runs. He won World Series titles with the team in 2004 and 2007 and was named World Series MVP in '04.
If Ramirez, now 54, lands a job as a hitting coach, it would be his first foray into coaching in the big leagues. He spent the 2014 season with the Chicago Cubs Triple-A affiliate, the Iowa Cubs, as a player-coach, where he worked with Red Sox All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras. After the 2014 season, he joined the Cubs front office as a hitting consultant through 2016.
Ramirez was also set to serve as a player-coach for the Sydney Blue Sox of the Australian Baseball League in 2020-21, but uncertainty around the COVID-19 pandemic meant he never appeared in a game.
Should the Red Sox hire him?
The Red Sox did little to answer any questions about the state of their coaching staff, many of whom were working under interim tags, in Monday's end-of-season press conference. However, given his reputation as a clubhouse annoyance and his repeated suspensions for PED use, it seems unlikely any team would take a chance on bringing Ramirez in. It feels especially unlikely that Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, who did not play with Ramirez, would bring in the should-be Hall of Famer as the team increasingly shifts its hitting philosophy to a more analytically based approach.
That said, after third baseman Caleb Durbin turned his season around with an outside hitting instructor and with key pieces like Contreras openly questioning the team's reliance on analytics, what's the risk?
Throughout the season, plenty of questions arose about Breslow and the coaching staff's ability to communicate and connect with the players. At the bare minimum, Ramirez represents a guy who knows what it takes to succeed at the highest level. At best, he's a voice INSIDE the organization to help players who don't feel like they're getting the most out of the analytical approach, like Durbin.
That's not to say they should hand him the keys to the hitting department, but bringing him in as a hitting consultant seems like one of the lowest-risk moves you can make. If it doesn't work out, you simply move on.

item.content:encoded:
If you're not already a card collector, Red Sox fans, here's the quick version of what product sports cards enthusiasts are going crazy over right now. Bowman Chrome is Topps' flagship prospect release, the one product every year built specifically around getting a player's first-ever card into the hobby before he's played a single big-league game. Think of it like a company's IPO. It's the first moment the public gets to invest or collect a piece of a player’s career, before anyone really knows what it'll become.
That's the appeal, and it's also the risk. Some of these names turn into stars. Some never sniff the majors at all. Either way, this is the top of the sports card market right now, and some of these prices have gotten astronomical. You have to truly believe in these prospects to justify what you're paying for a shot at them.
The 1st Bowman class, Roman Anthony rookie cards, and how to collect Red Sox legends
Boston has four 1st Bowman cards this year, all likely the cheapest they’ll ever be simply because nobody outside the organization and minor league baseball enthusiasts know most of these names yet. Here's a rough rule of thumb worth keeping in mind: the higher the signing bonus, the more attention collectors tend to pay, and that logic really kicks in once a bonus crosses $750,000. If a front office was willing to bet that kind of money on a teenager's upside, it's a fair question why a collector wouldn't take the same signal seriously.
Dawvris Brito signed for $1.2 million as the headliner of the 2026 international class, a shortstop with quick-twitch athleticism and triple-digit exit velocities already, and if there is a speculative play, I’d be playing in Brito’s camp. Garielvin Silverio signed for $1.4 million as a physical, left-handed-hitting corner outfielder with raw power, but is likely limited to a corner outfield spot due to lack of speed and athleticism.
Louis Andujar is the wild card of the group, and exactly the kind of story that makes chasing a bargain fun. Boston signed him for just $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic, a number so modest he barely registered outside the organization. He quietly hit .280 with a .974 OPS in the Dominican Summer League, then hit .410 with a 1.233 OPS in his stateside debut this year, good enough for FCL Hitter of the Week honors. If the $750,000 rule (that I made up completely) tells you who the industry believes in, Andujar is the opposite bet entirely, a near-free flier already outplaying his price tag.
The last name in this class comes with the best story attached. Enddy Azocar signed with Boston in January 2024 for just $40,000 out of Venezuela. He climbed all the way to the Red Sox's No. 5 prospect by this summer, hitting .286 with 18 home runs and 11 stolen bases in 85 games, right before Boston shipped him to Baltimore in the Rutschman trade. He hasn't missed a beat since, hitting .467 with a 1.238 OPS in his first 15 at-bats for High-A Frederick, and he's now the Orioles' No. 8 prospect. His 1st Bowman card will always have a Red Sox jersey, a snapshot of the last piece of a $40,000 bet Boston made and then dealt away for a franchise catcher.
Connelly Early carries that same wrinkle in a smaller way. Boston shipped him to the Nationals this July in the Curtis Mead deal, yet his Red RC in this release still has him in a Red Sox uniform. If you're a true Red Sox fan who likes owning a piece of the ones that got away, these are exactly those cards.
If you’re a top prospect hunter and have slept on Franklin Arias, this release gives you more chances to buy into his market, just not the way you'd expect. He doesn't get a 1st Bowman card this year (his 1st came last year), but he shows up with a prospect auto and two inserts as one of the sport's top prospects. If his original 1st Bowman wave passed you by, this is a more affordable way back into his market before he's an everyday big leaguer.
If you believe in Roman Anthony, the rest of this checklist is built for you. This year has been riddled with injury, a hand issue that kept him out for months. But zoom out. Boston signed this guy to an eight-year, $130 million extension back in August 2025, running through 2033 with a 2034 option and escalators that could push the value to $230 million.
That's a franchise betting on a 22-year-old being the face of this roster for the next decade, and Anthony's Red RC, Chrome Rookie Auto, Jumbo Chrome Autograph Relic, and Across the Seams autograph all reflect that same belief. If you're the kind of collector who buys into a player rather than a single season, the injury noise shouldn't scare you off so much as it should make this exact window the moment to buy in, before he's healthy and the price reflects it.
Every team in this release gets a shot at the future. Not every team has the history and memories that Red Sox fans have and names like Manny Ramirez, Roger Clemens, and Pedro Martínez in the same checklist should be like a slice of heaven. Ramirez lands in the Bowman Garbage Pail Kids (GPK) insert, a fitting nod to one of the most feared right-handed bats this franchise has ever run out. Clemens goes a step further with a base GPK card and an autograph version, and Pedro shows up in the Final Draft insert. None of these are prospect chases, and none will likely come cheap either, but they're closer to a tribute set than an investment. For a fanbase that grew up on these names, that's a fun thing to pull, regardless of cost.
Prices are always inflated in the first few weeks. Anthony's cards will likely cost the most, so waiting a month for the market to settle isn't unreasonable if you're patient. But Brito, Silverio, Azocar, and Andujar are cheap speculative buys worth grabbing now, and the Manny, Clemens, and Pedro pulls are worth paying up for if the fun of the rip matters more to you than the price tag.
